What Kind of Story Is The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats?

The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats is a Brothers Grimm tale in which a wolf tricks the little goats while their mother is away, but the mother teams up with her youngest to rescue them. It teaches both stranger awareness and family love.

Curious about the plot of The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats? Let's explore the lessons of The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats alongside the pictures.

content.alt: The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats - The original story
content.text:
The Original Story

This is a European folktale (KHM 5) recorded by Germany's Brothers Grimm in 1812. The wolf softens its voice and whitens its paws to deceive the goats; the youngest survives by hiding inside a clock, and the mother cuts open the sleeping wolf's belly to rescue her children — a wonderfully satisfying ending that is the heart of the tale.

content.alt: The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats - Plot summary
content.text:
Plot Summary

The mother goat warns, "Beware the wolf with the rough voice and black paws." The wolf softens its voice and whitens its paws with flour to trick the little goats. The youngest, hidden inside the clock, tells the mother, and she cuts open the sleeping wolf's belly to rescue her children — and the family is happy once more.

content.alt: The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats - The lesson it teaches
content.text:
The Lesson This Tale Teaches

At its heart lie not being fooled by a stranger's sweet words and appearance, and a love that protects family to the very end. Talk it over with your child — "What would you do if someone said Mom sent them?" — and connect it to safety awareness.

content.alt: The Wolf and the Seven Little Goats - How to read it aloud
content.text:
How to Read It Aloud

Play the wolf's fake voice and the mother's real voice differently. Ask "How can you tell if it's really Mom?" to build discernment, and decide on a secret knock just for your family together. Best suited for ages 4 to 7.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What age is it good for?
A. It suits ages 4 to 7. Its clear safety message about being wary of strangers makes it a great choice.

Q. Won't the wolf scenes be scary?
A. Versions for young children draw the wolf gently and end on a satisfying note, so children can watch with peace of mind.

Q. What activities pair well with it?
A. Deciding on a family secret signal, a "spot the fake voice" game, and making safety-promise cards are all great.
